title: The Tax Instalment That's Still Priced for Last Year's Business
linkedin:
Your PAYG instalment notice just landed for the September quarter. If the number felt wrong, you were probably right.

Most PAYG instalments are calculated from your last assessed tax return, not from how this year is actually tracking. It is a rearview mirror figure, applied to a business that never stands still.

For a business holding steady, that lag barely matters. For a business that has changed pace, a new contract, a lost customer, a meaningful price rise, a one-off strong year that will not repeat, the gap between the notice and current trading becomes real cash flow risk in both directions.

Slow down, and the instalment keeps asking for a figure sized to a stronger year, pulling cash the business needs for wages and suppliers now. The overpayment comes back, but only as a credit months later, after it has already forced a decision on the overdraft.

Speed up, and the instalments paid through the year understate the real tax position. The gap surfaces as one larger bill at tax time, sometimes with interest attached if the shortfall runs beyond the ATO's safe harbour margin.

None of this is a mistake by your bookkeeper or BAS agent. They are applying the ATO's formula exactly as designed. It is a structural feature of a system anchored to last year, sitting under a business that is not standing still.

A registered agent can lodge a variation before the 28 October due date. The commercial layer alongside that is different: folding the accurate number into a rolling cash flow view so it never lands cold in the same fortnight as payroll and super.
